Bernard Bolzano era un sacerdote de Prag: Bernard Bolzano was a priest in Prague, removed from his chair for his ideas, when in 1817 they published a proof of this theorem that leaned on no picture at all, only on the definition of continuity. Until then it had been taken as obvious: how could a curve pass from below to above without crossing? Bolzano held that the obvious has to be proved too, because that is where the mistakes hide. Almost nobody read it. Half a century later Weierstrass reached the same ideas independently, and it was then that the priest from Prague was recognised as having got there first.

It has consequences that look like conjuring tricks. At some moment in your life you were exactly one metre tall: your height changed continuously from a little less to a little more. A square table with equal legs on an uneven (but continuous) floor can always be turned until it stops wobbling: turning it a quarter turn makes the function measuring the wobble change sign. And at every instant there are two opposite points on the equator at exactly the same temperature. All three are the intermediate value theorem. And the first of its serious uses is the one seen above: bisection, the safest root-finding method there is, which [[av-numerico|numerical analysis]] carries all the way.
